title: Healthy and unhealthy relationships
keyIdea: A healthy relationship rests on respect, trust, honesty and the freedom to say no. Relationships sit on a spectrum from healthy to unhealthy to abusive. Warning signs include jealousy that stops you seeing friends, checking your phone, put-downs and pressure after a no. Coercive control is a pattern of these over time, and it is a crime. Setting a clear, calm boundary is assertive. If you or a friend are not safe, tell a trusted adult or call Childline on 0800 1111.

kid: A healthy relationship feels safe. You can be yourself. You can see your friends. When you say no, the other person listens and stops. These are sometimes called green flags.
Some signs are red flags. A partner who reads your messages or gets angry when you see friends is trying to control you. Jealousy like that is not proof of love. It is a warning sign.

Relationships sit on a line: healthy, then unhealthy, then abuse, like threats. Control is often a pattern, not one bad day. When put-downs and tracking happen again and again, it is called coercive control. It is against the law.

A boundary is what you will and will not do. Say it clearly and calmly, then stick to it. If you or a friend are not safe, tell a trusted adult or call Childline on 0800 1111. In danger now, call 999 or 911.
adult: This lesson follows the DfE statutory guidance for Relationships and Sex Education in secondary schools in England. It covers what makes a relationship healthy: trust, respect, honesty, kindness, boundaries and consent. It also covers how to spot unhealthy and abusive behaviour. Coercive control has been a crime in England and Wales since 2015. The PSHE Association plan for ages 14 to 16 covers the same ground.

The lab shows relationships on a line, not as good or bad. Sulking and guilt-trips are unhealthy. When they turn into a pattern of tracking, cutting someone off from friends, put-downs and threats, it is abuse. Students learn to look at what keeps happening over time. One bad day, or one kind gesture, tells you very little.

A common mistake is to think jealousy shows love. Many teens say constant checking is a sign of caring. Another is to think abuse must be physical, so control by phone or by words is missed. Students also often think kind days cancel out the bad ones. That is how control keeps going.

The boundaries step shows assertive replies: short, calm and clear about what the student will or will not do. Be careful not to mix up assertive with aggressive. On getting help, students practise listening without blame and telling a trusted adult. Confronting a partner, or promising to keep it secret, can make things more dangerous.

visual.caption: Green flag or red flag? Drag each one, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Puts you down in front of others
Threatens to leave if you see friends

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort red and green flags, use the healthy–abusive spectrum, spot control across a week and set a boundary.

practice.prompt: Which is a sign of a healthy relationship?
choices: You can say no and it is respected
They decide who you can see
practice.hint: Which one leaves you free to make your own choices?
practice.explain: Respect means your no counts. Choosing who you see or taking your passwords is control.

practice.prompt: Jay's partner checked Jay's phone {n} times a week for {w} weeks. How many checks is that in all?
practice.hint: Multiply the checks each week by the number of weeks.
practice.explain: {n} times {w} is {=n*w} checks. When it keeps happening, it is a pattern of control, not a one-off.

practice.prompt: Jealousy that stops you seeing friends shows they really care. True or false?
choices: False, it is a warning sign
practice.hint: Does it give you more freedom, or less?
practice.explain: Caring gives you space. Jealousy that cuts you off from friends is a warning sign of control.

practice.prompt: In a week, Mo had {c} days with put-downs or tracking. How many of the 7 days were free of them?
practice.hint: Take the control days away from the 7 days.
practice.explain: 7 take away {c} is {=7-c}. Kind days do not cancel the {c} control days. The pattern still matters.

choices: A pattern of control, threats or put-downs over time
pool.hint: Think about what keeps happening, not one day.
pool.explain: Coercive control is a repeated pattern. It can be emotional or digital, not just physical, and it is a crime.

pool.prompt: Someone says no. What is the respectful thing to do?
choices: Act hurt so they change their mind
pool.hint: Consent is given freely. Can it be worn down?
pool.explain: Accept the no. Pushing or guilt-tripping is pressure, and consent given under pressure is not freely given.

pool.prompt: Sam asks for your password to prove you trust them. Which reply is assertive?
choices: "I keep my passwords private. That is not about trust."
Give it so Sam is not upset
pool.hint: Assertive means clear, calm and firm.
pool.explain: A calm, clear no sets the boundary. Giving in teaches them your no can be pushed; shouting can make things unsafe.

pool.prompt: A friend says their partner scares them. Best first step?
choices: Listen, then tell a trusted adult
pool.explain: Listen without blame and get a trusted adult involved. Confronting the partner or keeping it secret can increase the risk.

pool.prompt: Where does 'threatens to share your photos if you end it' sit?
pool.hint: Is this a threat that uses fear to control you?
pool.explain: It is abusive and it is a crime. Sharing or threatening to share intimate images is against the law.

pool.prompt: They are kind most days but cut you off from friends. Is it healthy?
choices: Yes, the kind days cancel it
pool.hint: Kind days can sit inside a pattern. What keeps happening?
pool.explain: Kind days and apologies often sit inside controlling patterns. The repeated isolation is the warning sign.

pool.prompt: A partner sent {p} angry texts an hour for {h} hours because Jay did not reply. How many texts?
pool.hint: Multiply the texts each hour by the hours.
pool.explain: {p} times {h} is {=p*h} texts. Demanding instant replies is monitoring, a warning sign of control.

pool.prompt: Jay noted {a} controlling moments on Monday and {b} on Tuesday. How many in total?
pool.hint: Add the two days together to see the pattern.
pool.explain: {a} plus {b} is {=a+b}. Writing moments down helps show a pattern to a trusted adult.

pool.prompt: Which number is Childline in the UK?
pool.hint: 999 is for danger right now. Which is the free helpline for young people?
pool.explain: Childline is 0800 1111, free and confidential. Call 999 (or 911 in the US) if someone is in danger now.

pool.prompt: Your partner wants your location shared all the time. What is it?
pool.hint: Is it checking you got home, or watching you all the time?
pool.explain: Constant tracking is monitoring, a warning sign. Caring is checking you got home safe and letting it go.
